title: Why you do it
hookLine: self-determination theory: we persist longer when motivation comes from within (Deci and Ryan)

cards: A doctor's advice, written on a slip of paper: sit quietly for two minutes a day. Down the hall, someone else sits for the same two minutes because the quiet helps them be gentler at home.
Same posture, same timer, same bell. From the outside, nothing tells them apart. The difference only shows up if someone asks a single question: why are you doing this?
Two psychologists built a whole theory around that question, and it sorts these two sitters in a way that matters.

teach.b: First, the theory. Edward Deci and Richard Ryan built what they call self-determination theory. Its starting point: motivation isn't one thing with a volume knob.
It comes in kinds. Some reasons feel imposed from outside: a reward, a threat, someone watching. Some feel like your own.
In their research, the second kind tends to go with sticking at things longer and getting more out of them. Second, the middle ground. People sometimes hear this as only do what's fun.
The theory says something more useful.

teach.h: A REASON YOU'VE MADE YOUR OWN.
teach.b: Between pure pressure and pure enjoyment sit reasons you've made your own: I don't love every sit, but I value what it does. Deci and Ryan put that kind, a value you've taken in and agree with, on the side of the self.
A reason doesn't have to be pleasant to be yours. Third, the guilt trap.
They also describe reasons that live inside your head but still work like pressure: I should, I'll feel bad if I skip.
Guilt can get someone to the cushion for a while; the theory treats it as a shakier engine than a value they actually hold. Fourth, an older voice.

teach.h: A WHY CAN BEAR A HOW.
teach.b: The philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche wrote, roughly, that someone who has their own why can bear almost any how. He wasn't writing about habits. But the shape fits: a reason you own makes the dull days easier to carry.

how: People who draw on self-determination theory often write down, in their own words, what a practice gives them, and return to that reason on days when the practice feels like an obligation.

games.q: what does “why you do it” mean?
o: the kind of reason behind a practice, which affects how it lasts
the excuse you give others when you skip a practice
how badly you want something, measured by your effort

games.q: inside why you do it: tap the pairs.
p: a why can bear a how

s: the theory says only fun activities last
a value you've taken in counts as your own reason, even when the task isn't fun.
guilt comes from inside, so the theory counts it as your own reason
'I should, or I'll feel bad' still works like pressure, even inside your head.
the theory says motivation comes in kinds, not just amounts
Deci and Ryan sort reasons by how much they feel like your own.

games.q: a friend says she sits every morning 'because I'm supposed to.' what would self-determination theory listen for next?
o: whether a reason of her own sits underneath.
whether someone checks up on her.
games.why: the theory cares about the kind of reason: a value she holds herself tends to last longer than 'supposed to.'

practice: Ask quietly, and not with the answer you'd give at a party or one that starts with 'I should': when this practice goes well, what does it give me, or the people around me?
Let an answer come in a few words, calmer mornings, patience with my mother, a minute that's mine, and hold it for a breath or two. Then let it rest, and sit with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Why you do it. The kind of reason behind a practice matters: a reason you own tends to outlast pressure and guilt. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my own reason. Under an 'I should,' a reason of your own is sometimes hiding. Go gently.

sources.ref: Ryan & Deci, "Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being"
Twilight of the Idols, "Maxims and Arrows" 12
